title: Vujčić argues that expanding market finance requires safeguards for forced selling
summary: Europe needs a larger role for market financing, Boris Vujčić argued on 16 November, but the benefits would be harder to sustain if non-banks responded to a common shock by selling the same assets. Deeper capital markets can give firms more ways to finance investment and distribute risks more widely. Concentrated portfolios, short-term financing and redemption promises can also make liquidity disappear precisely when markets need it. The ECB vice-president used the prospective financing of artificial intelligence and the changing market for government bonds to show why bank-by-bank supervision cannot answer every question about financial stability (opening and final sections).

Vujčić distinguished the November environment from the previous year. Concerns about AI had initially centred on high equity valuations. Large cloud and infrastructure firms were now borrowing heavily, private equity and credit funds were financing projects, and firms in the supply chain had begun financing their own prospective customers. The speech cites projected cumulative capital spending of USD 5.5 trillion by major US technology firms by 2030. That is a spending projection. It cannot be read as the amount of new debt that will be issued or the value of cash flows from unaffiliated customers. The combination of supplier finance and commitments to buy hardware or services makes the latter especially difficult to establish. IPO volumes relative to US GDP were on track to exceed the dot-com peak. Past associations between heavy issuance and market peaks informed his concern without providing a date for a correction.

Meanwhile, rising energy costs had helped push headline euro area inflation from 3.8% in September to 4% in October. Underlying inflation remained broadly stable, and wages had yet to show a material response. Output continued to grow in the third quarter but at a slower pace than in the second. Weakening confidence and higher borrowing costs could partly offset inflationary pressure by weighing on demand. This combination mattered for sovereign debt. A weaker growth outlook can strain public finances even as inflation concerns and increasingly price-sensitive investors keep long yields high. Leveraged hedge funds provide liquidity in normal markets. Japanese investors might reduce euro area holdings if yields at home rise. Vujčić raised the possibility that corporate and government borrowers would compete for financing, without claiming that large corporate issuance had already displaced a specific public borrower.

Funds' holdings of AI equities and bonds provide a route from commercial disappointment to redemptions. If indebted funds have to sell, the effect can reach sovereign or repo markets even when the original news concerns technology earnings. Banks have strong aggregate capital and liquidity, and Vujčić judged that regulatory buffers were not currently restricting lending. He favoured retaining those buffers. He also regarded the risks in private credit as contained at present while emphasising gaps in information about bank and insurer connections, liquidity and leverage (sections on key risks and non-bank resilience).

The proposals depend on the source of fragility. Investment funds should align redemption terms with the liquidity of assets. Money market funds need larger buffers that can actually be used in stress. For hedge funds, Vujčić suggested considering limits on leverage, minimum margins or haircuts for securities financing. Better preparation for collateral calls and cross-border information sharing would help authorities see where the same risk has accumulated. These were proposals raised by the speaker. The keynote announced no new binding requirements.

questions.question: How much of the projected AI spending requires external finance from Europe?
questions.detail: The speech gives a cumulative US capital-expenditure projection and describes fast-growing borrowing, but neither number identifies who ultimately funds each project. Compare provider cash flows and commitments with debt issuance, leases and private fund exposures. For a European credit or bank investor, the location and seniority of each claim matter more than the headline capital-spending total.

questions.question: Where would a fund redemption spill into otherwise liquid sovereign markets?
questions.detail: Vujčić describes overlapping AI and sovereign exposures and leveraged trading in repo. The same fund need not hold both assets for a spillover if counterparties share a bank or funding source. Compare holdings, liquidity buckets, redemption terms and financing counterparties using the supervisory and transaction records available to the authorities. The timing of cash calls would help distinguish losses from forced sales.

questions.question: Would greater liquidity buffers remain usable when investors withdraw?
questions.detail: The keynote recommends both higher and more usable money market fund buffers. A published buffer level alone gives little information about whether a manager will run it down under pressure. Compare fund rules, supervisory expectations, past redemption experience and managers’ cash-management disclosures. These details would help investors judge whether a rule change could reduce the need to sell into a falling market.
